spec.title: Repository workspaces, parallel plans and branch integration

status.comment: Owner request of 2026-09-16: multiple independent plans in one Git repository and optional worker worktrees within a plan. Verify with ZapMockAgent and real Git before live models.

p.identity: A repository, a registered project, a plan context and a physical worktree have separate stable opaque identities. Git's canonical common directory identifies a repository binding on one execution host, not the repository's global identity. A project can be a subdirectory within that repository, and distinct projects can share the repository. Each plan context owns its conversation, coordinator, execution state, events and planning-service binding; it is not the planning algorithm's adopted-plan revision. Multiple contexts may belong to one project and repository. Existing default contexts retain their identities and checkout binding. Creating an independent plan prepares its owned worktree before any coordinator starts, preserving the project's relative directory within the repository. Algorithm-plan binding may initially be pending: preparing a working directory and starting the coordinator must remain possible before that coordinator creates or adopts an algorithm plan.

p.preparation: Workspace preparation is an algorithmic server operation with a durable operation identity, explicit immutable commit basis and observed result. The service generates the owned branch and worktree path under a trusted root, records ownership and verifies common directory, branch, HEAD and project cwd before publishing readiness. Retries reconcile that exact operation and never adopt an unrelated directory. A worker inherits the plan workspace by default or requests an isolated child workspace; the server resolves and persists its actual cwd before launch. Uncommitted parent changes are not silently copied, discarded or stashed. Native children claim isolated-workspace support only when the host can actually set and attest their cwd.

p.assignment: Each work attempt records its plan context, actor, task and known semantic target references together with the prepared workspace and commit basis. Repeated attempts preserve assignment history. Actor identity, workspace identity and a branch name are distinct; unknown assignments stay unknown. Source and target contexts are carried through every command and navigation callback, including portfolio views. A plan's configured source and planning authority follow its own workspace rather than the project's default directory.

p.integration: Integration is a durable operation bound to source and target workspace identities and exact observed commit OIDs. Prepare the integration in a separate owned worktree. The requesting plan owns the candidate and its resolution task; the target retains separate admission and write authority. Candidate, worker, graph references and diff share that one owning context even when the recorded target is the original checkout in another context. A clean merge produces a candidate for authorized review; a conflict produces a bounded resolution task in the integration worktree. Neither a clean Git merge nor a worker's report automatically accepts the semantic task. Promotion requires the accepted candidate, unchanged expected target HEAD, a clean target including protection for ignored files, and exclusive permission to write that actual target. Promote by fast-forward without overwriting ignored files. A busy target queues or refuses promotion rather than allowing competing writes. Changed target basis invalidates the preview and requires a new preparation.

p.recovery: Persist operation intent and state before side effects. After interruption, reconcile actual Git and workspace state with the recorded identity and commit basis before retrying. Preserve failed and conflicted artifacts for inspection. The first release does not automatically delete branches or worktrees, rewrite history, force-push, reset user changes or perform automatic stashing. Project Pause and Stop retain workspace assignments and pending integrations. Garbage collection and remote execution are separate future capabilities.

p.multi-user-hosts: Owner addition of 2026-09-16: preserve an extension path to several people, accounts and computers communicating over a network. Human principals and memberships, provider-account references, logical agents, coordinator sessions, execution hosts and process incarnations remain distinct. Shared commands are authorized at the server, carry an accountable author, use scoped idempotency and optimistic revisions, and retain reviewer identity. Paths and provider credentials belong to a protected host binding; another client or host cannot use them merely by knowing a public object ID. Connecting another clone to an existing repository requires explicit trusted registration, not equality of remote URLs or local path strings. Current execution is local-only and refuses unsupported remote operations explicitly. A host-execution port and ownership lease/epoch contract permit later remote dispatch and fencing; the current implementation does not claim distributed locking, remote Git synchronization, account federation or multi-user authentication. Per-client selections remain separate from shared plan state.

p.contribution-trust: Long-term owner vision: people may contribute their own execution hosts and model-account capacity to a shared project. Resource availability grants no authority to change the accepted project. A contribution retains submitting principal, execution host, assignment and attempt, source basis, produced artifacts and evidence origin. Execution, reporting, testing, reviewing and admission are separate authorities. A future trusted team-lead agent can coordinate review of potentially malicious contributions, but prompts and the contributor's own success reports never replace server authorization, independent checks or an explicit admission decision. Worktree separation is not a security sandbox. Execution of untrusted code will require a separately designed isolation boundary and secret policy. Credentials stay with the resource owner; capacity contribution does not pool or reveal account keys. Current local trusted execution implements none of the future public resource marketplace, hostile-code sandboxing or contributor admission services.

p.resource-grants: The future scheduling boundary separates a task's requirements from a participant's revocable resource grant and from the selected execution attempt. A grant may restrict projects, operations, model profiles, budget, concurrency and expiry; resource ownership and project authority are checked independently. Host disconnection leaves an observed or uncertain attempt, not an assumed failure or permission to replay irreversible effects. Existing scoped request identities, attempt provenance, lease epochs and separate integration admission must remain usable when a local execution port is replaced by a remote one. This is an extension constraint, not a requirement to implement a distributed scheduler in the current delivery.

p.projection: All Lens clients share server-owned plan, workspace, assignment and integration data. Quick Lens supports selecting multiple plans of one project, shows the responsible actor and workspace on work items and cards, and represents fork, integration and conflict-resolution operations as stable semantic nodes and relationships. Graph distance and layout never imply elapsed time or completed integration without evidence. Events retain the full history and cross-reference the corresponding operation; notes and Trash preserve references to retired objects.

p.verification: Colocated deterministic scenarios use real Git in small disposable repositories and ZapMockAgent executors. Cover two top-level plans in one repository, inherited and isolated workers, preparation before agent launch, scoped file changes, clean integration, an actual conflict and resolution, stale or dirty target refusal, restart reconciliation and graph assignment/fork/join projection. The original checkout and other contexts remain unchanged by child work. No provider inference or developer credentials are required. Mock success does not establish vendor-specific native-worktree capabilities.
